title: Basic Plant Biology
summary: This lesson introduces the main parts of a plant, explains how photosynthesis works, and describes the plant growth cycle. Students will see how these concepts connect to everyday farming.
objectives: Identify and label the major parts of a plant
Explain the basic steps of photosynthesis
Describe the stages of a plant's growth cycle
Connect plant parts and photosynthesis to crop productivity
Predict how changes in light or water affect plant growth
prerequisites: No prior knowledge is required, but students should be familiar with basic biology terms like cell and energy.
why: Understanding plant biology is the foundation of agriculture. Farmers need to know how plants capture sunlight and turn it into food to choose the right crops and manage fields effectively.

In everyday life, plant health affects the food we eat, the air we breathe, and the environment. Knowing how plants grow helps people make better decisions about gardening, farming, and conserving natural resources.

sections.heading: 1. Plant Parts Overview
sections.body:
Plants are living machines made of a few basic parts, each with a special job.  
When we know the name of each part and what it does, we can see how a plant grows, how it makes food, and how farmers can keep crops healthy.

**Roots** are the part that grows down into the soil. Their main jobs are to hold the plant steady (anchoring) and to drink water and minerals (absorbing). Think of roots like the feet of a person: they keep you from falling over and bring in the nutrients you need from the ground.

**Stems** grow upward from the roots. They act like a highway, moving water and food between the roots and the leaves. A stem is also a support that keeps the leaves and flowers in the right position to catch sunlight and wind.

**Leaves** are the flat, usually green “solar panels” of the plant. Inside each leaf are tiny cells that capture light energy and turn it into chemical energy through a process called photosynthesis. This is how the plant makes its own food.

**Flowers** are the reproductive organs. They contain the parts that make pollen (the male part) and receive pollen (the female part). When pollen moves from one flower to another, seeds can form.

**Fruits** develop from the flower after fertilisation. They protect the seeds and often help spread them, for example when animals eat the fruit and later drop the seeds elsewhere.

Below is a very simple diagram that shows where each part sits on a typical plant:

```
   (Fruit)   (Flower)
        \     /
         \   /
          \ /
          Leaf
          |
          Stem
          |
          Root
```

> **Definition:** *Anchoring* – the action of holding a plant in place so it does not fall over, just like a tent stake keeps a tent upright.

> **Note:** Roots do not only take up water; they also gather minerals such as nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) that are essential for building proteins and DNA.

> **In daily life:** When you see a carrot in the grocery store, you are looking at a swollen root that stores food for the plant. Carrots are edible roots, while lettuce is an edible leaf.

> **Common mistake:** Many people think the stem “makes” food. In reality, the leaf does the food‑making, and the stem simply transports it.

The functions of these parts can be linked by a simple equation that describes the flow of water from roots to leaves:

$$
\text{Transpiration Rate} = \frac{\text{Water taken up by roots}}{\text{Leaf surface area}}
$$

This tells us that a larger leaf area usually means more water will leave the plant through tiny openings called stomata. Farmers use this idea to decide how much to water a crop.

Understanding each part helps us answer practical questions. For example, if a plant’s leaves turn yellow, the problem is often with the roots (maybe they are not getting enough water or nutrients). If the stem is weak and bends, the plant may need support, just like a tall tomato plant often needs a stake.

In summary, a plant is built from:

- **Roots** – anchor and absorb.
- **Stem** – support and transport.
- **Leaves** – capture light and make food.
- **Flowers** – create seeds.
- **Fruits** – protect and spread seeds.

When you can name each part and explain its role, you have the foundation for everything else you will learn about agriculture, from soil management to crop breeding.

sections.heading: 2. Roots: Anchoring and Absorbing
sections.body:
Roots are the hidden half of a plant, but they do most of the work that keeps the plant alive.  
First, think of a plant like a person standing on a trampoline. The feet (roots) hold the person steady and also pull up the air that the person needs to breathe. In the same way, roots **anchor** the plant in the soil and **absorb** water and nutrients that the plant uses to grow.

### How roots take up water  

Water moves from the soil into the root cells by a process called **osmosis**. Osmosis is the movement of water across a thin membrane from an area where there is more water (low solute concentration) to an area where there is less water (high solute concentration).  

The inside of a root cell contains dissolved sugars and minerals, so its solute concentration is higher than that of the surrounding soil water. Because of this difference, water flows into the root cells until the concentrations become more equal.

The rate at which water can move is described by the equation  

$$
J_w = L_p \, \Delta \Psi
$$  

where $J_w$ is the water flux (how much water passes per unit time), $L_p$ is the hydraulic conductivity of the root membrane (how easily water can pass), and $\Delta \Psi$ is the water potential difference between soil and root. A larger difference in water potential (for example, very dry soil) makes $J_w$ larger, pulling more water into the root.

### How roots absorb nutrients  

Nutrients are minerals such as nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K) that plants cannot make themselves. Roots absorb them through **active transport**, a process that uses energy (usually from sugars) to move nutrients against their concentration gradient— from low to high concentration.  

Think of a grocery store checkout line. If the line is short (low concentration of shoppers), people can move quickly through. If the line is long (high concentration), the store may open extra counters and use staff (energy) to move shoppers faster. In roots, transport proteins act like those extra counters, using energy to pull nutrients into the cells even when the soil has only a little of the mineral left.

### Why root health matters  

A healthy root system has many fine, hair‑like extensions called **root hairs**. These increase the surface area for water and nutrient uptake, much like a sponge with many tiny pores can hold more water than a smooth stone. If the root hairs are damaged—by compacted soil, pests, or disease—the plant cannot take up enough water or nutrients, leading to wilting, yellow leaves, and stunted growth.

> **Note:** Root health is not just about size. A small root system with many healthy root hairs can be more efficient than a large, woody root mass that lacks hairs.

### Everyday comparison  

Imagine watering a houseplant with a thin straw versus a wide hose. The straw (like a thin root) can deliver water directly to the plant’s base, but if the straw is blocked, no water gets through. The wide hose (like a thick, woody root) can carry a lot of water, but if the hose is old and cracked, it leaks and wastes water. Both need to be clear and functional for the plant to thrive.

### Simple steps to keep roots healthy in a garden  

1. **Loosen the soil** – Avoid compacted soil so roots can spread easily.  
2. **Add organic matter** – Compost improves soil structure and supplies nutrients.  
3. **Water consistently** – Too much or too little water stresses roots and reduces their ability to absorb nutrients.  
4. **Watch for pests** – Insects such as root maggots can damage root hairs; early detection helps prevent loss.

> **In daily life:** When you feel thirsty after a long walk, you know your body’s “roots” (blood vessels) are delivering water to your cells. Keeping your water bottle full is like keeping the soil moist for plant roots.

> **Remember:** Healthy roots = strong plant. If the foundation is weak, the whole structure suffers.

By understanding how roots anchor a plant and pull in water and nutrients, you can see why farmers and gardeners pay close attention to soil preparation, irrigation, and pest control. A robust root system is the first step toward a bountiful harvest.

sections.heading: 3. Leaves and Photosynthesis
sections.body:
Leaves are the “kitchens” of a plant.  
They sit on the outside of the stem, spread out like tiny solar panels, and turn light, air and water into food that the whole plant can use.

**Why leaves matter** – A plant cannot move to find food, so it must make its own where it is rooted. The leaf’s job is to capture energy from the sun and combine it with simple ingredients from the air and the soil. This process is called **photosynthesis** (photo = light, synthesis = putting together).  

> **Definition:** *Photosynthesis* – the chemical process by which green parts of a plant use sunlight to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugars (food) and oxygen.

### The three main ingredients

1. **Sunlight** – the energy source. Photons (tiny packets of light) strike the leaf surface and are absorbed by a green pigment called **chlorophyll**.  
   *Chlorophyll* is the molecule that gives leaves their green colour. It works like a solar panel: it captures light energy and passes it to the plant’s chemical machinery.

2. **Carbon dioxide (CO₂)** – a gas that plants take in through tiny openings on the leaf surface called **stomata** (singular *stoma*). Stomata are like tiny mouths that open and close to let gases in and out.

3. **Water (H₂O)** – drawn up from the roots through the stem and delivered to the leaf via tiny tubes called **xylem**. Water provides the hydrogen atoms needed for the food molecules.

### The basic chemical equation

When these three ingredients meet inside the leaf’s cells, they are rearranged into sugar and oxygen. The overall reaction can be written as:

$$
6\;CO_2 \;+\; 6\;H_2O \;+\; light\;energy \;\rightarrow\; C_6H_{12}O_6 \;+\; 6\;O_2
$$

In words: six molecules of carbon dioxide plus six molecules of water, using light energy, become one molecule of glucose (a simple sugar) and six molecules of oxygen.  

> **Note:** *Glucose* is the plant’s food. It can be used right away for energy or stored as starch for later use.

### How the leaf carries out the reaction

Inside each leaf cell are tiny, disc‑shaped structures called **chloroplasts**. Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and all the enzymes (protein helpers) needed for photosynthesis. The process occurs in two main stages:

1. **Light‑dependent reactions** – happen in the thylakoid membranes of the chloroplast. Here, sunlight splits water molecules into oxygen, protons, and electrons. The oxygen is released back to the air through the stomata – the same gas we breathe in.

2. **Calvin cycle (light‑independent reactions)** – takes place in the fluid-filled space called the **stroma**. Carbon dioxide from the air is combined with the hydrogen from the split water to build glucose.

> **In daily life:** The oxygen we exhale comes mainly from plant leaves. Every breath you take is a tiny thank‑you to photosynthesis.

### Why the leaf’s shape helps

Leaves are usually flat and thin. This shape maximizes the surface area exposed to sunlight while keeping the distance that carbon dioxide and water have to travel very short. Think of a solar panel: the larger the panel, the more sunlight it can catch. Similarly, a broad leaf catches more light, and the thinness lets gases diffuse quickly.

### Common misunderstandings

> **Common mistake:** Believing that all parts of a plant perform photosynthesis. Only the green, chlorophyll‑containing parts (mainly leaves) are efficient at this. Stems and roots may have some chlorophyll, but they are far less effective because they receive less light.

### Key take‑aways

- Leaves turn light, carbon dioxide, and water into glucose and oxygen.  
- Chlorophyll is the green pigment that captures light energy.  
- The overall reaction is simple to write but involves many tiny steps inside chloroplasts.  
- The food made in leaves travels through the plant’s transport system (the **phloem**) to feed roots, stems, fruits, and seeds.

> **Remember:** Without leaves performing photosynthesis, a plant could not grow, and the world would have far less oxygen and food. The next time you see a green leaf, think of it as a tiny factory turning sunshine into the energy that fuels life.

sections.heading: 4. Stems and Transport
sections.body:
The stem is the plant’s “highway” that connects the underground roots with the leafy “factory” above ground. Its main job is to move water, dissolved minerals, and the sugars that leaves make during photosynthesis. This movement happens in two special tube systems that run side‑by‑side inside the stem: **xylem** and **phloem**.

**Xylem** (pronounced “ZY‑lem”) is a set of dead, hollow cells that act like tiny straws. They pull water and minerals upward from the roots to every leaf. The driving force is **transpiration**, the slow loss of water vapor from leaf surfaces. When water evaporates from a leaf, it creates a tiny “pull” that is transmitted through the continuous column of water inside the xylem, much like sucking on a straw draws liquid up.

**Phloem** (pronounced “FLO‑em”) is a living tissue that carries the sugary food made in the leaves to the rest of the plant, especially to growing roots and developing fruits. Unlike xylem, phloem moves material in both directions, depending on where the plant needs food.

> **Definition:** *Transpiration* – the process by which water evaporates from the tiny openings (stomata) on leaf surfaces, creating a suction force that lifts water through the xylem.

The two transport systems work together but follow different rules. Water moves upward in the xylem because of a combination of **cohesion** (water molecules stick together) and **adhesion** (water sticks to the walls of the xylem cells). This is called the **cohesion‑tension theory**. The basic idea can be written as:

$$
\text{Water flow} = \frac{\Delta P}{R}
$$

where $\Delta P$ is the pressure difference created by transpiration and $R$ is the resistance of the xylem pathway. A larger pressure difference (more transpiration) or lower resistance (wider vessels) means faster water flow.

In the phloem, movement is driven by a pressure‑difference created by loading sugar into the phloem at the source (usually a leaf) and unloading it at the sink (root, fruit, or young shoot). This creates a high‑osmotic pressure at the source and a lower pressure at the sink, causing the sugary solution to flow. The equation that describes this is the **Münch pressure‑flow model**:

$$
\text{Flow rate} = \frac{\Delta \pi}{\eta}
$$

where $\Delta \pi$ is the difference in osmotic pressure between source and sink, and $\eta$ is the viscosity of the sap.

> **In daily life:** Think of the xylem as a garden hose that only lets water flow upward, while the phloem is like a delivery truck that can go to any part of the farm that needs food.

Why does this matter for farming? If a plant cannot move enough water, its leaves wilt and photosynthesis slows down, reducing yield. If sugar cannot reach the roots, the plant’s storage organs (like tubers or fruits) will be small. Farmers can help both systems by providing adequate water, avoiding compacted soil (which blocks xylem flow), and ensuring balanced nutrition so the phloem has enough sugar to transport.

> **Note:** Xylem vessels are dead cells, so they do not repair themselves. Damage from pests or frost can permanently block water flow, while phloem cells are alive and can sometimes heal small wounds.

A common misunderstanding is to think that water and sugar travel in the same tubes. In reality, they use separate pathways, which prevents the two substances from interfering with each other's movement.

> **Common mistake:** Assuming that water moves downwards in the stem because gravity pulls it. In plants, the cohesion‑tension mechanism can lift water many meters against gravity.

Remember that the stem’s transport system is a living “pipeline” that must stay clear and functional. Proper irrigation, gentle handling of crops, and avoiding soil compaction keep the xylem and phloem working efficiently, leading to healthier plants and better harvests.

sections.heading: 5. Reproductive Parts: Flowers, Seeds, and Fruits
sections.body:
Plants need a way to make the next generation, and they do it with three main parts: **flowers**, **seeds**, and **fruits**.  
Think of a flower as a tiny factory, a seed as a packaged baby plant, and a fruit as the delivery truck that carries the package to a new home.

**How a flower makes a seed**  
A flower is made of several pieces. The **stamen** (the male part) produces tiny grains called *pollen*. The **pistil** (the female part) holds the **ovary**, which contains one or more *ovules* – these are the tiny eggs that can become seeds.  

When a pollinator such as a bee lands on a flower, it brushes pollen onto the sticky surface of the pistil called the **stigma**. The pollen then grows a tube down the **style** (a tube that connects stigma to ovary) and reaches an ovule. Inside the ovule, the pollen fuses with the egg cell. This fusion is called **fertilisation**.  

> **Definition:** *Fertilisation* – the joining of a male pollen cell with a female egg cell, creating a new cell called a *zygote*.

The zygote develops into an **embryo**, the tiny plant inside the seed. At the same time, the ovary tissue begins to change and will become the fruit.

**From seed to new plant**  
A seed is not just a dormant egg; it is a self‑contained kit that lets the embryo start growing when conditions are right. A typical seed has three parts:

1. **Embryo** – the future plant (shoot, root, and leaf primordia).  
2. **Endosperm** or **cotyledons** – stored food that feeds the embryo.  
3. **Seed coat** – a protective outer layer.

When a seed lands in soil with enough water, oxygen, and the right temperature, the seed coat softens and the embryo begins to grow. The first root (called the **radicle**) pushes down to anchor the plant and absorb water. The first shoot (the **plumule**) pushes upward to reach light. As the seedling grows, it uses the stored food until it can make its own through photosynthesis.

> **Note:** A seed will not germinate if any one of the three requirements—water, oxygen, or suitable temperature—is missing.

**Why fruit matters**  
The fruit is the mature ovary that surrounds the seeds. Its main job is to protect the seeds while they develop, but it also helps spread them far from the parent plant. Fruits can be **fleshy** (like apples or berries) or **dry** (like nuts or pods).  

- **Fleshy fruits** attract animals. When an animal eats the fruit, the seeds pass through its digestive system and are deposited elsewhere, often with a ready supply of fertilizer.  
- **Dry fruits** may open on their own and let the wind carry the seeds away, or they may cling to animal fur.

> **In daily life:** The bananas we eat are actually berries, and the hard “seed” inside a peach is the plant’s embryo ready to grow a new peach tree.

Humans also use fruits as food because they are rich in sugars, vitamins, and fiber. By harvesting fruits, we obtain both nutrition for ourselves and a way to plant new crops when we keep the seeds.

**Putting it all together**  
1. **Flower** → produces pollen and ovules.  
2. **Pollination** → pollen reaches stigma.  
3. **Fertilisation** → pollen + egg → embryo.  
4. **Seed formation** → embryo + food + coat.  
5. **Fruit development** → protects seeds and aids dispersal.  

> **Remember:** The whole cycle—from flower to fruit— is the plant’s strategy for making copies of itself and spreading those copies across the landscape. Understanding this cycle helps farmers choose the right varieties, manage pollinators, and harvest fruits at the optimal time for both yield and seed quality.

sections.heading: 6. The Plant Growth Cycle
sections.body:
The plant growth cycle is the series of steps a plant goes through from the moment a seed lands in the soil until the plant dies and returns nutrients to the earth. Understanding each stage helps farmers know when to water, fertilize, or protect crops, and it also shows why certain weeds appear at predictable times.

**Stage 1 – Germination**  
Germination is the first “wake‑up” of a seed. When a seed absorbs water (a process called *imbibition*), enzymes inside the seed become active and start breaking down stored food. This food fuels the growth of a tiny root (the *radicle*) and a shoot. The seed’s coat softens, and a small shoot pushes upward toward the light.

> **Definition:** *Germination* – the process by which a seed takes up water and begins to grow into a new plant.

**Stage 2 – Seedling**  
A seedling is a young plant that has just emerged from the soil. It has a short stem, a few true leaves, and a primary root system. At this point the plant is very delicate; it needs plenty of moisture and protection from extreme temperatures or herbivores. Farmers often use mulch or shade cloth to keep seedlings safe.

**Stage 3 – Vegetative Growth**  
During vegetative growth the plant focuses on building leaves, stems, and roots. Photosynthesis – the conversion of light energy into chemical energy – happens mainly in the leaves. The more leaf area a plant has, the more food it can make, which in turn supports faster growth. This stage is where most of the crop’s biomass (the total amount of plant material) is produced.

> **Note:** The rate of vegetative growth can be estimated with the simple equation $$\text{Growth Rate} = \frac{\Delta \text{Biomass}}{\Delta \text{Time}}$$ where ΔBiomass is the increase in plant weight over a given time interval.

**Stage 4 – Flowering**  
When a plant has accumulated enough energy and the environmental cues (like day length or temperature) are right, it switches from vegetative growth to reproductive growth. Flowers appear, each containing the organs needed for pollination. Successful pollination (transfer of pollen from male to female parts) is essential for seed and fruit formation.

**Stage 5 – Fruiting**  
After pollination, the flower’s ovary develops into a fruit, and the fertilized ovules become seeds. The fruit protects the seeds and often helps disperse them. For many crops, the fruit is the part harvested for food (e.g., tomatoes, beans, wheat kernels). The timing of fruit set determines when the harvest will occur.

> **In daily life:** Think of the fruiting stage like a bakery finishing a loaf of bread. The dough (flower) must rise (be pollinated) before it can be baked (turned into fruit) and finally sold (harvested).

**Stage 6 – Senescence**  
Senescence is the plant’s aging phase. Leaves turn yellow, nutrients are moved from the leaves back into the stems and roots, and the plant gradually dies. Farmers may leave the dead material on the field to decompose, returning nutrients to the soil for the next planting cycle.

> **Remember:** Each stage follows the previous one in order; skipping a stage (for example, trying to harvest before fruiting) will not produce a usable crop.

---

### Simple Timeline Graphic

```
Germination → Seedling → Vegetative Growth → Flowering → Fruiting → Senescence
|          |            |                |          |          |
Day 0      Day 5-10    Weeks 2-8        Weeks 8-12  Weeks 12-16  Post‑harvest
```

This linear timeline shows the typical order and approximate timing for many temperate crops. Adjustments are needed for different species or climates, but the basic sequence remains the same. By recognizing where a crop is on this timeline, farmers can apply the right care at the right time, leading to healthier plants and better yields.

sections.heading: 7. Applying Plant Biology to Farming
sections.body:
Plants are not just green decorations; every part of a plant tells a farmer when to plant, what to feed it, and when to harvest. By looking at roots, stems, leaves, and flowers, we can make smarter decisions that increase yield and reduce waste.

**Root clues for planting time**  
When a seed sprouts, the tiny root (called a *radicle*) pushes down into the soil. If the soil is too cold, the radicle grows slowly or stops, and the seed may die. Farmers therefore check the **soil temperature** before sowing. A simple rule is:

$$\text{Plant when soil temperature} \ge 10^\circ\text{C (for most cool‑season crops)}$$  

If the temperature is lower, the seed will stay dormant. This is the same idea as waiting for the right moment to bake a cake: the oven must be hot enough before you put the batter in, otherwise the cake will not rise.

> **Note:** Soil temperature can be measured with a cheap probe or by feeling the soil with your hand after a few minutes of digging. Warm, moist soil feels soft and gives a slight resistance.

**Leaf health and fertilizer use**  
Leaves are the plant’s solar panels. They capture sunlight and turn it into food through *photosynthesis*. The green pigment *chlorophyll* is the key player. When chlorophyll is abundant, leaves are dark green and the plant is making lots of sugar. If leaves turn yellow, it often means the plant lacks nitrogen, a nutrient needed to build chlorophyll.

Think of nitrogen like the fuel in a car. When the tank is full, the car runs smoothly; when it is low, the engine sputters. Farmers can apply nitrogen fertilizer when they see the first signs of yellowing, but only after confirming that the soil actually lacks nitrogen. Over‑fertilizing is like over‑filling a gas tank – it wastes money and can pollute waterways.

> **In daily life:** A quick “leaf test” is to compare the newest leaves to older ones. If the newest leaves are lighter green than the older ones, add a modest amount of nitrogen (about 20 kg N ha⁻¹ for many cereals) and re‑check in two weeks.

**Stem thickness and water management**  
The stem transports water from the roots to the leaves. A thick, sturdy stem usually means the plant has enough water and can support a heavy fruit load. Conversely, a thin, wilted stem signals water stress. Farmers use this information to schedule irrigation.

Imagine a garden hose: if the hose is kinked (thin stem), water cannot flow well, and the plants at the end will dry out. By measuring stem diameter with a simple ruler or caliper, a farmer can decide whether to turn on the irrigation system.

> **Common mistake:** Assuming all crops need the same amount of water. Different species and growth stages have different water needs; a wheat field at the jointing stage needs more water than the same field at maturity.

**Flower and fruit development for harvest planning**  
Flowers are the plant’s reproductive organs. When pollination succeeds, flowers turn into fruits or seeds. The timing of flower emergence tells the farmer when the crop will be ready to harvest. For example, a soybean plant that flowers on day 45 after planting will typically be ready to harvest around day 110. This relationship can be expressed as:

$$\text{Harvest day} \approx \text{Flowering day} + 65$$  

(Exact numbers vary by variety and climate.) By recording the first flower date, a farmer can predict the harvest window and arrange labor, storage, and market sales in advance.

> **Remember:** Keep a simple log: date of sowing, date of first leaf, date of first flower, and expected harvest. This log becomes a valuable calendar for future seasons.

**Putting it all together**  
1. **Check soil temperature** before sowing – ensures the radicle can grow.  
2. **Watch leaf color** – guides nitrogen fertilizer applications.  
3. **Measure stem thickness** – informs irrigation timing.  
4. **Record flowering date** – predicts harvest day and helps plan market logistics.

By linking each plant part to a specific farming decision, the farmer moves from guesswork to evidence‑based management. The result is healthier crops, lower input costs, and a smoother harvest season—just like following a recipe step by step leads to a tasty meal.

examples.title: Identify plant parts of a bean seedling
examples.given: A bean seed has just sprouted. List the visible parts and state their main function.

steps.label: Observe
steps.text: Look at the seedling and note the root, stem, and leaves; this shows the basic organs.

steps.label: Identify
steps.text: Name each part: root, stem, leaf.

steps.label: Function
steps.text: Explain: root anchors and absorbs water; stem supports and transports; leaf makes food by photosynthesis.

examples.answer: Root (anchoring & water uptake), Stem (support & transport), Leaf (photosynthesis).

examples.title: Classify leaf types and predict photosynthetic efficiency
examples.given: Two crops are grown: wheat with narrow, parallel-veined leaves and soybean with broad, net-veined leaves. Which leaf type is likely to have higher photosynthetic rate per leaf area and why?

steps.label: Compare
steps.text: Note leaf shape and vein pattern of each plant.

steps.label: Relate
steps.text: Broad, net‑veined leaves have more surface area for light capture.

steps.label: Reason
steps.text: More surface area generally allows more chlorophyll and gas exchange, increasing photosynthesis per area.

examples.answer: Soybean leaves (broad, net‑veined) are likely to have higher photosynthetic efficiency per leaf area.

examples.title: Design a simple irrigation decision for a field using root depth knowledge
examples.given: A farmer has two plots: Plot A planted with carrots (root depth ~30 cm) and Plot B with corn (root depth ~150 cm). The soil moisture sensor shows 20 % moisture in the top 30 cm and 35 % moisture from 30 cm to 150 cm. Decide which plot needs irrigation now and justify.

steps.label: Assess
steps.text: Determine the moisture available within each crop’s root zone.

steps.label: Compare
steps.text: Carrot roots are within the dry 20 % zone; corn roots extend into the wetter 35 % zone.

steps.label: Decide
steps.text: Carrots are likely water‑stressed, corn is not.

steps.label: Recommend
steps.text: Irrigate Plot A now; postpone irrigation for Plot B.

examples.answer: Irrigate Plot A (carrots) immediately; Plot B (corn) can wait.

practice.q: What are the two main functions of plant roots?
practice.a: 1. Anchoring – Roots grow into the soil and hold the plant steady so it doesn’t fall over. 2. Absorbing – Tiny root hairs increase surface area, allowing roots to take up water and dissolved minerals from the soil. Both functions are essential for plant stability and nutrition.

practice.q: Which part of the leaf contains most of the chlorophyll that captures sunlight?
practice.a: The chloroplasts are located mainly in the mesophyll cells, especially the palisade mesophyll, which is just below the upper leaf surface. These cells contain the green pigment chlorophyll that absorbs light for photosynthesis.

practice.q: Explain how water moves from the roots to the leaves through the plant’s vascular system.
practice.a: 1. Water is absorbed by root hairs from the soil. 2. It enters the root’s xylem vessels, which are like tiny tubes. 3. A negative pressure (tension) created by transpiration – the loss of water vapor from stomata on leaves – pulls the water upward. 4. Cohesion (water molecules stick together) and adhesion (water sticks to vessel walls) help maintain a continuous water column. 5. The water reaches the leaf’s mesophyll cells where it is used in photosynthesis or evaporates from stomata.

practice.q: Describe the role of flowers in the plant life cycle and name two main parts involved in seed production.
practice.a: Flowers are the reproductive organs of angiosperms. They attract pollinators or use wind to transfer pollen (male gametes) to the stigma (female part). The two main parts for seed production are: 1. The ovary, which contains ovules that become seeds after fertilization. 2. The stamens, which produce pollen. After fertilization, the ovary develops into a fruit that protects the seeds.

practice.q: A farmer notices that his wheat crop is stunted and the leaves are yellowing at the tips. Using knowledge of plant biology, list three possible physiological reasons for these symptoms and suggest one management practice for each.
practice.a: Possible reasons and management: 1. Nutrient deficiency – especially nitrogen or magnesium, which are needed for chlorophyll. Management: Apply a balanced fertilizer or a specific N‑rich fertilizer based on soil test results. 2. Water stress – either drought or waterlogged soil limiting root function. Management: Adjust irrigation to provide consistent moisture; improve drainage if soil is waterlogged. 3. Root damage from pests (e.g., nematodes) or disease reducing water and nutrient uptake. Management: Rotate crops and use nematode‑resistant varieties or apply appropriate soil fumigants following guidelines.

practice.q: Explain how the concepts of photosynthesis and transpiration are linked in the plant’s overall energy and water budget, and why both are important for crop yield.
practice.a: Linkage: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy (sugars) using CO₂ and water. Transpiration is the loss of water vapor from stomata, which creates a negative pressure that pulls water up through the xylem to the leaves. This water supply provides the raw material (H₂O) for the light‑dependent reactions of photosynthesis. At the same time, the opening of stomata for CO₂ intake inevitably causes transpiration. Importance for yield: Efficient photosynthesis produces more sugars, leading to more growth, grain, or fruit. Controlled transpiration helps cool the plant and transports nutrients, but excessive loss wastes water and can limit growth, especially in dry regions. Managing both (e.g., optimal planting density, irrigation, and selecting varieties with favorable stomatal behavior) maximizes biomass and ultimately crop yield.

recap: Plants are made of roots, stems, leaves, and reproductive parts, each performing essential jobs like anchoring, transporting water, making food, and producing seeds. Roots absorb water and nutrients through osmosis, stems act as highways using xylem and phloem, and leaves capture sunlight to run photosynthesis. Flowers turn pollen into seeds, which grow into new plants through the plant growth cycle, and understanding these parts helps farmers manage crops effectively.

key_terms.meaning: The underground part that anchors the plant and absorbs water and minerals.
The above‑ground support that transports water, minerals, and sugars between roots and leaves.
Flat green organ that captures sunlight and carries out photosynthesis.
Process where chlorophyll uses sunlight, carbon dioxide, and water to make sugars and oxygen.
Dead, hollow cells that move water and minerals upward from roots to leaves.
Living cells that transport sugars from leaves to other parts of the plant.
Reproductive structure that produces pollen and ovules, leading to seed formation.
The stage when a seed takes up water and begins to grow into a seedling.

quiz.q: What is the main function of roots?
options: Anchor the plant and absorb water
quiz.why: Roots hold the plant in place and take up water and nutrients.

quiz.q: Which tissue moves water upward in the plant?
quiz.why: Xylem consists of dead, hollow cells that act like straws to pull water up.

quiz.q: What pigment gives leaves their green colour and captures light?
quiz.why: Chlorophyll is the green pigment that absorbs sunlight for photosynthesis.

quiz.q: During photosynthesis, which gas is taken in from the air?
quiz.why: Plants use carbon dioxide as a carbon source to make sugars.

quiz.q: What part of the flower becomes the fruit after fertilisation?
quiz.why: The ovary develops into fruit, enclosing the seeds.

quiz.q: Which stage follows germination in the plant growth cycle?
quiz.why: After a seed germinates, the young plant is called a seedling.
